blocks.1: The stone crosses are our best-known historic monuments. When they came and who had them raised has been studied and pondered a great deal. One legend says that St Olav had the cross by the churchyard gate raised when he was here on a preaching journey with his brother Harald in 1023. This cross has been called the Olav cross. If the cross was raised in 1023, it may perhaps be connected with the introduction of Christian law into the Gulating law. A. Faye, who published “Norske folkesagn” (Norwegian folk legends, 1948), records a tradition that St Olav came to Eivindvik and stayed where the parsonage lies, and that he raised both crosses, one to consecrate the place for worship and the other “near an old sacrificial spring to destroy the heathen worship there”. Olav also commanded the people to build a church.
blocks.2: Holck also mentions the tradition that St Olav raised the crosses in his article in “Budstikken” referred to earlier, p. 270. Another legend I have heard says that King Olav, probably St Olav, shot 3 arrows from the assembly site, and where each of the arrows fell a cross was raised. According to what people say about where “the third cross” is supposed to have stood, these crosses would then have formed the corners of a roughly equilateral triangle.
blocks.3: Another legend says that the king shot all the red dots found on the crosses into them with his arrows.
blocks.4: There is also a legend that says: “Now it is no longer the Æsir but the White Christ who rules at the Gulating. Before him they proclaim the peace of the assembly beneath the holy cross. Then the bishop sang the Gloria from the old, fine royal booth that Håkon Adalsteinsfostre raised”, quoted from Birkeli's book “Norske steinkors i tidleg middelalder” (Norwegian stone crosses in the early Middle Ages), p. 189.
blocks.5: One person who has studied stone crosses closely is precisely Bishop Fritjov Birkeli. His book is very interesting, and he also writes a good deal about the crosses in Eivindvik. Letters between him and the parish priest Johannes Holten in the years around 1960 show that Birkeli came here several times to look at the crosses and the place where they stand. He also travelled widely to other places where there are crosses, including the British Isles, where the models for our crosses are to be found. In addition he read a great deal of both Norwegian and British history and familiarised himself thoroughly with what he writes about. He therefore has a broad and sound background for the ideas he puts forward.
blocks.6: The oldest written record found of the two crosses is a note from 1626 in “Arnamagnæanske samlinger” (the Arnamagnæan Collection), folio 370, which says, among other things: “In the diocese of Bergen, in Nordhordland, at Evendvijg parsonage there are 2 stone crosses: the first stands by the church and is five Zealand ells high, two ells wide and four fingers thick; the other stands 288 ells to the north of the first, and is 4 Zealand ells high and 2 ells wide, with a small cross carved on it...”
blocks.7: The same record includes the legend that King Olav the Holy “is said to have shot these red spots or stones into them” and that “the monks are said to have walked around them with cross and banner twice a year, which is Holy Cross Day in the spring and Holy Cross Day in the autumn, and then blessed field and meadow.”
blocks.8: The dates of the feasts of the Cross were 3 May and 14 September. At these masses the monks are said to have walked in procession between the crosses. I have heard that the spring mass was to pray for a blessing on the crops, and in the autumn it was a mass of thanksgiving for the year's harvest.
blocks.9: It has been said that the cross by the churchyard gate once stood down by the sea. In his “Report on an inspection in Gulen 7–12 June 1975”, Professor Knut Helle says, among other things: “The placing of the crosses is discussed so thoroughly here because in recent times a tradition has arisen that Dean Dahl moved the cross by the church up from the sea (Flolid 1918; cf. Hannaas 1921–22; Østgulen 1961, p. 99). From what has been said above it follows that this tradition cannot be correct”.
blocks.10: By “what has been said above” Helle refers to the measurements he made and compared with the distances given in the record of 1626, and with measurements later made by Dahl. Helle also considered it “rather unthinkable” that Dahl himself would not have mentioned such a move when he showed Bishop Neumann the crosses and when he later wrote about them. As to the idea that the crosses were moved to Eivindvik from somewhere else, Helle says there is no evidence for anything of the kind. He goes on: “We do not know their history before 1626, but there is no basis for claiming that they stand anywhere other than where they were first raised”.
blocks.11: There is a tradition that an earlier priest moved the baptismal font, which stood next to the cross by the churchyard gate, down to the sea, and that Dahl moved it back up. “Possibly we have here the seed of the clearly incorrect tradition that one or even both of the stone crosses were also moved up from the sea”, Helle writes.
blocks.12: Of the 60 stone crosses in all that Birkeli says are registered, no fewer than 54 belong to Western Norway, from Jæren in the south to Sunnmøre in the north. All the stone crosses “that still exist” belong to Rogaland, Hordaland and Sogn og Fjordane. The explanation is probably that the custom of raising crosses, which came to us from the British Isles, reached Western Norway first, where contact with Britain was greatest, and before this custom of raising such tall, free-standing crosses really reached other parts of the country, other practices had taken over in worship.
blocks.13: The Anglian cross at Krossteigen, with a small Latin cross carved between its arms.
blocks.14: In the book mentioned above, Birkeli says that the cross by the churchyard gate belongs to a small group he calls the “Norse-Celtic” type. They have straight arms and characteristic semicircular armpits. Of the crosses in this group he says on p. 239: “But all three reveal that those who made them had a clear knowledge of the Celtic style.” On p. 241 he writes: “The cross is so elaborate that a priest from a ‘Celtic’ area must have overseen its making.” Of the Celtic crosses in Norway he writes on the same page, among other things: “..the only certain thing is that they represent a mission and church link between Western Norway and the ‘Celtic’ part of the British Isles.”
blocks.15: As mentioned, legend says that this cross was raised by St Olav in 1023. Birkeli says (p. 241): “...concluded that it must be connected with one of the episcopal royal missions led by Olav Tryggvason or Olav Haraldsson. Our hypothesis is that it is then more natural to guess at Olav Tryggvason than at Olav Haraldsson, since this is probably a cross at the Gulating. The other cross must then be regarded as a kind of assembly cross, and this ‘Celtic’ cross, with the baptismal font that tradition says belongs to it, was presumably a place the ‘assembly priest’ used as a place of worship from Olav Tryggvason's time onwards, before the church was built.”
blocks.16: Elsewhere in the book, p. 232, Birkeli writes, among other things: “Nor should we forget the tradition that Olav Tryggvason was baptised in the Scilly Isles..” These islands lie near an area where Norsemen had settled and where there are many simple crosses, and even clearly Celtic crosses.
blocks.17: In his article in “Urda”, Brømel says that the people were baptised and Christianised at the Gulating in 997. I have seen this year mentioned by others as well. Perhaps the cross and the font were placed there in connection with this great “mass baptism”?
blocks.18: But even though St Olav has probably, perhaps unjustly, had many legends and traditions attached to him because of the special status he gained after he was made a saint, I would mention that he too spent a great deal of time in the British Isles and could well have brought Celtic priests with him to Norway.
blocks.19: Of the cross up at Krossteigen, Birkeli says, among other things, on p. 242: “With its large, round and harmonious arcs between the arms of the cross, the characteristic straight end of each arm, and the slender, well-worked shaft, it may well be said to represent a simplified ‘Norse-Anglian’ type”. Of the Anglian type of cross Birkeli also says on p. 235: “It joins all the arms with long, broad lines in various variations, but as a rule keeps the straight line at the end of each arm”. He also says that “the Anglian cross was partly very simple, partly lavishly carved”. Among Anglian crosses many examples have been found of decoration in the field between the arms, including carved crosses, but Birkeli has not seen the same type as in the cross at Krossteigen, where the shaft of the carved cross disappears “elegantly” into the shaft of the main cross. Birkeli says the small carved cross is a Latin cross.
blocks.20: On p. 183 Birkeli writes that the cross at Krossteigen is in its form “unique in Norway and has a clearly foreign character”, and further that the cross is very finely made, “a very elegant form”, and that it “must have been made by a skilled carver.” He believes we must bear in mind that crosses were made in England, Ireland and Scotland after several centuries of contact with European civilisation and Christianity, whereas in Norway the crosses were raised almost at the very start of Norwegian contact with Christianity. “It is clear that there is no native tradition” (p. 238). He considers it highly likely that Norway got its “cross impulses” from the British Isles.
blocks.21: In E. Bjordø's book on “Eivindvik kirke” (Eivindvik church) it says on p. 7 that in front of the cross at Krossteigen there lay a stone table – “perhaps, as the folk legend has it, it was a sacrificial table”.
blocks.22: I would like to add that many large stone slabs have been found at the parsonage. In both the main outbuilding and the cowshed at Krossteigen, stone slabs were used, among other things, as partitions between the stalls.
blocks.23: The cross at Krossteigen has a remarkable position: it stands so that at the winter solstice (22 December) the sun just reaches the whole cross; one might say the cross stands at the edge of the shadow. “The sun never sets over the cross at Krossteigen” was a saying that the parish priest Johannes Holten tested on 22 December 1961. That day the weather was clear, and it turned out that the saying was right. In a copy of a letter dated 5 January 1962 I see that Holten wrote, among other things: “I was at the spot and saw that what had been said held true. The stone stands in the slope in such a way that the sun's eye covers the whole stone. This does not last long. It is a matter of minutes, then there is shadow again.” Several others have also checked this and say that it is true.
blocks.24: Birkeli leans towards the view that it was Håkon Adalsteinsfostre who raised this cross. Håkon, who was brought up in England, probably knew Glastonbury well, which at that time was one of England's most important spiritual centres, with the famous Glastonbury Abbey. Birkeli maintains that Håkon's bishop came from this region, and it is then reasonable to believe that the priests in Håkon's missionary attempt also came from there, or from other central parts of England. Birkeli claims that in Somerset, the county where Glastonbury lies, there was a small Norwegian settlement. He points out that the fishing boats in one area there still have an unmistakably Norwegian shape to this day. Perhaps the link here with Norway may have something to do with the monastery that is said to have been in Eivindvik?
blocks.25: Many have mentioned the crosses in their “writings”. Dahl writes, for example, on p. 503 of his article in “Budstikken” in 1824: “The cross that stands by the church, and which seems older and more simply carved than the other one standing to the north, makes it unmistakably clear that it was raised before the church was built, to consecrate the place as a gathering place for worship, or only to christen the place itself. As is well known, such crosses were very common in the Middle Ages, especially where there had not yet been time or opportunity to pay for the building of churches.” As an example of “the care with which such crosses were maintained” he mentions that there were farms that had been “given” for the upkeep of crosses. After the Reformation the crosses were no longer used as before, and the farms were released. He mentions the farm “Herrandstvedt” in Kvinnherad, which was given “back” in the 16th century by Bishop Geble in Bergen. We all know the expression “he went neither to cross nor to church”, which also goes back to the crosses being a Christian gathering point.
blocks.26: Many agree with Dahl that the cross here by the churchyard gate served as a gathering point for church rites and as a sign that it was now Christianity that had taken power at the place where the old heathen temple stood. The religious rites continued in the same place as before, but now it was the White Christ they worshipped instead of the Æsir. Birkeli writes, among other things, on p. 227 that Archbishop Theodore, who organised the church in England in the second half of the 7th century, took the view that “a cross should be raised where there had been an altar”.
blocks.27: As for the cross at Krossteigen, it seems that most people believe it was placed there to transfer the attention and the “power” from the holy spring (now called St Olav's spring) and the sacrificial grove below it to the symbol of Christianity. The cross was probably also connected with the assembly; the peace of the assembly was now proclaimed beneath the fine, well-placed Christian sign of the cross. Bishop Neumann, among others, writes about this (“Budstikken” 1824, p. 377): “..one is raised by the sacrificial spring mentioned, but the other by the church, as a sign of Christianity's victory over the overthrown idolatry.”
blocks.28: The stone the crosses are made of has not been found here. Such stone is said to be found in Hyllestad municipality. Some believe the crosses were carved in Britain and shipped here finished, others that the priests/monks brought the material with them from there and carved the crosses on the spot, while still others believe the crosses were carved here from material fetched from Hyllestad.
blocks.29: The measurements of the crosses according to Birkeli's book:
blocks.30: The cross by the church: “The measurements above ground are: greatest length 2.75 m, the width across the top of the side arms 1.15 m and across the underside of the arms 1.05 m. This difference arises because the left side arm is somewhat damaged and slopes unevenly inwards. Each side arm is about 36 cm wide. The top piece is about 33 cm wide. All three pieces are evidently meant to be equally wide all the way. The shaft is about 39 cm wide down at the ground. Both side arms are about 40 cm long, apart from the damaged part of the left arm. The distance between all four armpits is 36 cm. The armpits are circular and very well made. The diameter of all four armpits is about 10 cm. The thickness of the cross is about 6–7 cm at the top and about 13–15 cm at the bottom.”
blocks.31: The Celtic cross, the Olav cross, outside the churchyard gate.
blocks.32: The cross at Krossteigen: The measurements are given on p. 183 as follows: height on the south side 2.49 m, on the north side 2.24 m, greatest width “from arm to arm is about 1.30 m. The outermost width of the arms is 42, 43 and 48 cm respectively. After a few cm of normal width, the rest of the arms are shaped into a large semicircle. The diameter of the upper western arm is 39 cm, and the diameter of the upper eastern arm is 44 cm. The two lower arms merge evenly from the rounded curve into the shaft. The thickness varies from 8 to 10 cm. In the middle of the front of the cross a raised Latin cross is carved. It stands out 1 to 2 cm from the rest of the stone surface. The shaft of this small cross widens downwards and gradually disappears elegantly into the surrounding stone surface. The length of this carved cross is 63 cm, the width 55 cm.”
blocks.33: According to tradition, as mentioned, there was yet another cross in Eivindvik, the one called “the third cross”; compare the legend of the arrows St Olav shot from the assembly site. The clairvoyant Anna Elisabeth Westerlund said when she was here in 1983 that there had been a third cross, and that it came before the two crosses that stand here now. I have seen a record of older people, interviewed by Andreas Midttun, who claim to have seen or heard of this cross. Bernt Austgulen, who was then over 100 years old, told me a few years ago that he remembered the cross standing in the slope east of the new churchyard, on the north side of the road up to Haugane. It has been claimed that the cross still stood there in the mid-1930s. Øysten Hovden, parish priest in Gulen 1927–1937, wrote in the parish register that on Tuesday 14 April 1936 the members of the “Gulating study circle” met at the parsonage to look more closely for any remains of the cross. The shoemaker Ole Ellingsen, about 70 years old, pointed out the place where the cross had stood. Ellingsen then lived in the house that still stands up by the stone wall right above the spot. He told Hovden that “the last time he noticed it was some time after Easter in 1899”. Hovden's conclusion was this: “It nevertheless proved impossible, by digging and careful probing with iron bars at the spot, to find anything that recalled this cross or the ‘foundation’ it had stood on.”
blocks.34: Hovden also names a number of people who said they had seen the cross standing there themselves; among others, the local historian Karl Gåta is said to have remembered the cross well from the 1880s and 90s. Hovden writes of the position of the cross: “This cross is said to have stood in the slope towards Haugane – east of the new churchyard – some 5–6 metres north of the old public road that ran here.” This agrees with the position I have heard from others, and which Westerlund also “saw”. According to what people have said, the cross was “somewhat smaller” than the other two, it stood askew and one of its arms was broken off. This also agrees with what Westerlund said. Westerlund further said that the cross was broken up even more and used in a building – in a staircase or a wall – and she believed that the house in which the remains of the cross were used is the house up on the farm above where the cross is said to have stood.
blocks.35: Per Linge believes that the stone crosses here are much older than the introduction of Christianity at the Gulating. He also thinks that they, together with the wall around the parsonage (which he believes was an enclosure around the capital that lay here (compare the piece on the name)), are part of an old Turkic system of measurement, and that Dean Dahl's work on the wall was to restore it. He says the small carved cross between the arms of the cross at Krossteigen may have something to do with Christianity. What we call the third cross may have been a cross, or a similar marker, serving as a survey point on a straight line between the cross by the churchyard gate and the end of the wall by the sea at Midtunvågen, and it must have stood close to the house at farm no. 15, holding no. 31 at Haugane.
blocks.36: As can be seen from the 1626 record in the “Arnamagnæan Collection” quoted earlier, only two crosses in Eivindvik are mentioned there.
blocks.37: In his “Erindringer af mine Reiser” (Memories of my travels), Ivar Aasen writes of his visit here in 1843: “.... among relics of antiquity there are two large stone crosses, as well as a large baptismal font of stone”. Perhaps the third cross was so badly damaged that it was not registered as a proper stone cross?
blocks.38: In Amund Helland's book on Nordre Bergenhus county, part two, printed in 1901, p. 310, it says: “In Evenvik churchyard there are 3 grave slabs of ancient form. One of these, now broken, has on its back a raised cross with double arms, the lower arm shorter than the upper. The second of these stones is decorated with mouldings and a raised ridge along the middle and is among the very rare ones. The third is without decoration. All three are narrower at the lower than at the upper end and are 2 to 2 ½ ells long. On the churchyard wall stands a stone cross, about 1 ½ ells high and 1 ¼ ells across the arms, with a hole in the middle.”
blocks.39: What can have become of these things?
